Drama/Thriller, 15 min

01 — The pitch

The logline.

Rose and Matt's marriage is on the rocks. In a desperate attempt to save the relationship, Matt takes Rose deep into the wilderness for a weekend camping trip. Alone together, it quickly starts to feel more like a trap than a romantic weekend getaway.

Then Rose gets separated from Matt. As night closes in and she desperately tries to find shelter, a terrifying thought begins to take hold: What if Matt left her here on purpose?

She is the type of actor who thrives on delivering whatever the scene requires, whether that means playing it straight or chewing on the scenery. 03 — The crew! (so far)

The crew.

Photo of Jonathan Michael Mahoney — to be supplied by Jon

Jonathan Michael Mahoney Director of Photography

Our film will be lensed by the brilliant Jonathan Michael Mahoney! Jonathan has shot multiple features, shorts, commercials, music videos and experimental films. He is a graduate of California Institute of the Arts (CalArts) and FAMU (Film and TV School of the Performing Arts in Prague, Czech Republic), with an emphasis on 35mm cinematography. Most recently he worked as a camera operator on Avatar: Fire and Ash. Jonathan had the honor of being selected by Kodak to be an official 16mm film stock tester for Kodak's Vision 3 250D stock before its commercial release, and is so excited to be shooting 16mm again!

04 — The film! (literally!)

Shot on 16mm.

Oh, and did I mention I plan to shoot this on 16mm film?

This is a key part of what we're raising money for. When all is said and done, shooting this on film will cost about $1,000 more than shooting on digital, but the results will be worth every penny.

Film is intention. Film is a magic trick. A literal illusion. Some people love working with digital because it gives them more options to work with in the editing room. I'm not interested in having more to work with. I'm interested in getting the takes we need. We won't have much time regardless.

Put it this way. While I've seen so many movies shot digitally that look better than so many movies I've seen that are shot on film, at the end of the day, I firmly feel that film at its best is still consistently better than digital at its best.

And we're shooting in the wilderness! Talk about looking great on film! I want to see the rich greens of the trees, the texture of skin, through the grain of 16mm.

If anyone would like to read my extended passionate rant about film and why it's important (and I know at least SOME of you do!), click here.

Hyperlinked essay

Why film.

When I was in film school making my first short films, shooting on actual film seemed to be my good luck charm. These were invariably my best works compared with most of what I shot digitally. I don't think it's an accident. Film is what makes me want to get up in the morning. It's precious and therefore demands precision. It brings a different level of focus to the set. As much as I love digital when it's done well, it's not ultimately what I signed up for. It's hard to get me excited about it in even remotely the same way. I didn't come to this conclusion overnight, though. I wasn't always like this…

It was around the time I was in film school when movies first began to transition from being shot on film to being shot on digital, and the feelings of me and my friends were…confused? Digital suddenly gave us access to make work in a cheap and easy way that had never before been possible, and yet these didn't look like films as we understood them (I'm being generous). Were we excited about this new and easy access? Or were we on the raw end of a bait-and-switch, where now those dreams of looking through the lens of a Panavision camera like Steven Spielberg seemed further than ever?

The first few years of digital cinematography had some of us feeling cautiously optimistic. Film was still the standard, and so the standard was high, meaning people tended not to mess with digital unless they were damn confident they could reach that bar. And top directors like David Fincher, Steven Soderbergh and Michael Mann were among the first to get their hands dirty, enthusiastically so, making the waters seem potentially safe for the rest of us…

But then something happened. Digital became the default. Not an option, or an alternative, or simply a new tool (which I've long felt is the best way to view it). Instead, it became thought of as a cheaper option than film, and as more films made on digital by great directors did continue to get made, those great-looking movies became justification for all movies (or almost all) to get shot on digital, because by that point most people couldn't tell the difference anyway.

And now? People don't go to the movies anymore. Okay, so they do, but at a fraction of what the numbers used to be. People are always so quick to point to streaming and Peak TV as the culprit, yet Christopher Nolan's "The Odyssey" is still selling out showtimes in 70mm months into its release, to say nothing of its sales worldwide, and I believe there's a direct connection. Christopher Nolan has always been one of the biggest evangelists for celluloid, along with people like Quentin Tarantino, and there's a reason seeing their movies in theaters always feels like events.

The next time you go to your local cinema, take a look at the bright parts of the screen. Nine times out of ten you can see the wavy patterns of the silver screen itself. It almost looks dirty, but you don't see those patterns and lines when film is being projected, because the silver screen was designed specifically to have film projected onto it, not digital. I've noticed that even if a movie is projected digitally, it still looks better on the big screen if it was originally shot on film.

Have I mentioned I love film?

To repurpose the Men's Warehouse tagline, "You're gonna love the way it looks. I guarantee it."

The ask.

We are humbly asking for donations of anything you can give! No amount is too big or too small, and every single person who donates will be credited onscreen by name.

Our goal is to raise $20,000 to make and distribute the film. Pre-production will take about 8 weeks and we are planning to shoot in mid-January in the greater Los Angeles area, so our aim is to reach our goal by November 15th!

If we do reach our goal, however, you can still donate past that date, right up through production and post-production! More resources mean more can go up on the screen, so please forward this to any and everyone you think may be interested!
